'''Vera Huckel''' (May 10, 1908 – March 24, 1999) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[Aerospace engineering|aerospace engineer]]. She was one of the first female [[Computer (occupation)|computers]] and engineers at the [[National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics]] (NACA), now known as [[NASA]]. She worked at the [[Langley Research Center|Langley Aeronautical Laboratory]] and conducted research on [[Sonic boom|sonic booms]] created by [[Supersonic aircraft|supersonic flight]]. She was involved in the transition away from human computers and wrote the program for the first electronic [[computer]] used at NACA.

==Biography==
Huckel was born in 1908. She studied math at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and graduated in 1929.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Daily Press: Hampton Roads News, Virginia News & Videos |url=https://www.dailypress.com/ |access-date=2021-09-21 |website=dailypress.com}}</ref> After living in California for ten years, she was hired as a computer at the Langley Aeronautical Laboratory in Hampton, Virginia. She had filled out an application for the role only because she had driven friends to Langley to be interviewed as computers.<ref name=Loff>{{cite web |last1=Loff |first1=Sarah A. |title=When the Computer Wore a Skirt: Langley’s Computers, 1935–1970 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/langleys-computers-1935-1970/ |website=www.nasa.gov |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |access-date=30 April 2026}}</ref> Before the invention of electronic computers, these human computers, who were mostly women, would do the time-consuming calculations necessary for successful flights.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=50 YEARS: FLYING HIGH IN A MAN'S WORLD |url=https://www.dailypress.com/news/dp-xpm-19921108-1992-11-08-9211080018-story.html |access-date=2022-07-26 |website=Daily Press|date=8 November 1992 }}</ref> She was one of three female engineers at the NACA Memorial Langley Aeronautical Laboratory.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dean |first1=LaToya |title=Celebrate the Role of Women in NASA History |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/stennis/celebrate-the-role-of-women-in-nasa-history/ |website=www.nasa.gov |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |access-date=30 April 2026}}</ref>

Computers had to take the [[Civil service entrance examination|civil service examination]] and most had at least a bachelor's degree. In the 1940s, computers were classified as "sub-professional" in which a junior computer could make $1,400 a year and a chief computer $3,200 a year. Many of the men with similar qualifications were hired as junior engineers which paid $2,600 a year. Despite the sub-professional status, the role paid much better than most jobs available to women at the time.<ref name=Loff/>

She also worked as a supervisory mathematician and aerospace engineer during her time at NACA/NASA. By 1945 she had been promoted to section head in charge of up to 17 other women.<ref name=WNHM/>

She helped NACA make the switch from hand calculations to electronic computers. She wrote the program for the first electronic computer used by NACA.<ref>{{cite web |title=NASA Computer Scientist Profiles |url=https://challenger.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/FL_Minecraft-Coding-NASA-Computer-Scientist-Profile-Cards.pdf |website=challenger.org |publisher=Challenger Center |access-date=30 April 2026}}</ref> She also worked on theories of [[aerodynamics]]. As a mathematician, she was involved in the testing of sonic booms in supersonic flight.<ref name=":2" /> She would travel to the test sites in the western United States to calculate the mathematics of the test flights.  If she was unable to travel, the data was sent to her in Virginia as she was the only person trusted to perform the calculations.<ref name=WNHM>{{cite web |title=The Women of NASA |url=https://www.womenshistory.org/exhibits/women-nasa |website=www.womenshistory.org |publisher=National Women's History Museum |access-date=30 April 2026}}</ref>

Huckel retired from NASA in 1972 after working there for more than 33 years.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

She was active in the [[Soroptimist International|Soroptomist]] Organization, the [[American Association of University Women]], and volunteered with the Hampton [[United Way]].<ref name=":1" />

Huckel died at 90 years of age on March 24, 1999, in [[Newport News, Virginia]], where she had lived for more than 60 years. She was buried in [[West Laurel Hill Cemetery]] in [[Bala Cynwyd]], Pennsylvania.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Women's Activism NYC|url=https://womensactivism.nyc/stories/8655|access-date=2021-09-21|website=womensactivism.nyc|archive-date=2021-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028164552/https://womensactivism.nyc/stories/8655|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Publications==

* Morgan, Homer G., Harry L. Runyan, and Vera Huckel. "Theoretical considerations of flutter at high Mach numbers." ''Journal of the Aerospace Sciences'' 25, no. 6 (1958): 371–381.
* Morgan, Homer G., Vera Huckel, and Harry L. Runyan. ''Procedure for calculating flutter at high supersonic speed including camber deflections, and comparison with experimental results''. No. NACA-TN-4335. 1958.
* Hilton, David Artland, Vera Huckel, Domenic J. Maglieri, and R. Steiner. ''Sonic-boom exposures during FAA community response studies over a 6-month period in the Oklahoma City area''. No. NASA-TN-D-2539. 1964.
* Hilton, David A., Vera Huckel, and Domenic J. Maglieri. ''[https://www.google.com/books/edition/Sonic%20boom%20Measurements%20During%20Bomber%20Tr/dGG9Zdz29PgC Sonic-boom measurements during bomber training operations in the Chicago area]''. NASA-TN D3655 National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 1966.
* Henderson, Herbert, Vera Huckel, and Domenic J. Maglieri. ''[https://www.google.com/books/edition/Variability%20in%20Sonic%20Boom%20Signatures%20Mea/2M7ja11jQQsC Variability in Sonic Boom Signatures Measured Along an 8000-foot Linear Array]''. NASA-TN D5040 National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 1969.
